faq.a1: Yes. Sound events live in HKCU, the part of the registry that belongs to your own user account, and that is the only place Chimer writes. No system file is replaced, no DLL is patched, and nothing runs elevated. The worst outcome of a pack you dislike is a sound you dislike.
faq.a2: Yes, and you do not have to remember what they were. A restore point is saved before every apply, holding the raw value and type of each event exactly as Windows had it. Events that were silent come back silent — Windows spells silence as an empty value, and roughly a third of a stock install is silent.
faq.a3: No. Everything happens in your own user hive, so Chimer never asks for elevation. It also means the change follows your account rather than the machine: anyone else signing in to the same PC keeps their own sounds.
faq.a4: Yes. Build a custom pack by naming it and choosing a .wav for each event you care about. Custom packs stay on your machine — nothing is uploaded, and there is no account to create.
faq.a5: Windows 10 version 1809 or later, and Windows 11. Chimer uses the WebView2 runtime already present on those versions, so there is no extra runtime to install. It does not run on macOS or Linux, which have no equivalent sound scheme to rewrite.

h.text: Pick a pack, hear it before you commit, and apply the whole scheme at once. Your old sounds are backed up, so you can go back whenever you want.
h.title: Change every Windows sound
how.intro: Windows keeps its sound scheme in the registry, one entry per event — starting up, errors, notifications, emptying the Recycle Bin. Chimer edits those entries directly, so a new scheme takes effect straight away: no restart, no sign-out.
how.manualText: You do not need an app for this. Windows exposes the same settings under Control Panel → Sound → Sounds, where you can assign a .wav to one event at a time and save the result as a named scheme. Chimer exists because that dialog handles a single sound per visit, gives you no way to preview a whole scheme, and keeps no copy of what you replaced.
how.oneText: Thirty schemes are available, from the Windows 98 chime through XP, Vista, 7, 8 and 10, plus the thirteen Windows 7 bonus themes and the Microsoft Plus! packs. Every sound plays on this page and in the app, so nothing changes before you have heard it.
how.threeText: Each apply leaves a restore point holding the exact previous value of every event it touched. Restoring writes them back as they were. You can also swap a single event instead of a whole pack, or build a pack from your own .wav files.
how.title: How to change
how.twoText: One click writes the whole scheme at once. Chimer snapshots every event it is about to touch before the first write, and if any single event fails it rolls back the ones it already wrote — a pack is never left half-applied.

nf.p: The address may have changed, or the link is wrong. The shortcuts below cover everything the site has.
pv.p1: Chimer reads and writes the sound-scheme keys in your user registry (HKCU) and reads the audio files of the packs installed with the app. Nothing else.
pv.p2: No account, no login, no telemetry, no machine identifiers and no usage analytics. No personal data leaves your computer.
pv.p3: The only network connection is the optional update check, which queries the releases page and can be turned off in Settings. It sends no information about you or your system.
pv.p4: Backups of your previous scheme live in a folder inside your user profile. You can delete them at any time; the app never sends them off the machine.
pv.p5: Chimer is free and open source under the MIT licence. The repository shows exactly which keys are read and written.
pv.sub: Chimer is a local app. No account, no server, no usage data collected.
